articles.sourceTitle: Kimi K3.1 Pro and K3.1 Pro Highspeed
articles.title: Kimi K3.1 Pro Tech Blog: Advancing Open Intelligence
articles.text:
Introducing Kimi K3.1 ProWe're introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro, the first model in our new K3.1 series and our most capable 3T-class open-weight model to date, with a 1-million-token context window. It delivers substantial improvements across coding, 3D creation, financial research, and other agentic capabilities.
We are also releasing Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed, which delivers 2-3× the speed of K3.1 Pro for more responsive interactions.
Kimi K3.1 Pro and Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed are available today on Kimi.ai, Kimi Work, Kimi Code, and the Kimi API. The full model weights will be released by Nov 4.

Advancing the Frontier of Open Intelligence
Kimi K3.1 Pro is a post-trained version of Kimi K3, with substantially larger post-training compute. To enable large-scale joint RL across hundreds of downstream domains, we optimized every layer of the stack — the RL framework, long-context inference, training efficiency, sandbox infrastructure, rollout scheduling, and a shared platform for environment quality checks — so that each increment of RL compute delivers stable, predictable returns. As a result, K3.1 Pro achieves consistent gains in every domain.
Across coding, agentic, and knowledge benchmarks, K3.1 Pro matches or approaches the strongest proprietary models. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, which evaluates coding agents on realistic, resource-constrained terminal tasks using strict task-specific tests, K3.1 Pro scores 65.7%, ahead of GPT-6 Astra (58.2%) and narrowly behind Claude Opus 5.5 (66.4%). And on Kimi Code Bench 3.0 Long-horizon, our internal benchmark that tests coding agents' multi-step execution, tool use, and end-to-end problem solving across diverse engineering domains, K3.1 Pro scores 61.2%, above K3's 55.95%.

Coding
K3.1 Pro covers the full range of coding work, from quick fixes in real codebases to full-project builds. It also brings a more considered visual style to games and web experiences, and knows how to build them with the right tools.
K3.1 Pro works effectively across game engines such as Unity, Unreal Engine, and Godot, combining them with web search and 3D generation to create complete experiences. Its front-end pages, interactive Three.js scenes, and 3D assets show stronger composition, typography, animation, and polish. The examples below were created end to end by K3.1 Pro:

K3.1 Pro's long-horizon coding capabilities are also strengthened through large-scale reinforcement learning. In one internal test, it built a human walking dynamics simulator with integrated training and evaluation pipelines on top of human-atlas, an open-source anatomical model of the human body comprising 296 skeletal components, including cartilage, and 402 muscle components. Across 167 missions and 420 independent reviews, it analyzed experimental results, diagnosed problems, and iteratively refined the walking controller, enabling the simulated human to go from collapsing within seconds to walking continuously with alternating strides for 11.2 seconds. When reward shaping failed to improve arm motion, K3.1 Pro did not simply keep adjusting the reward: it ran open-loop probes of the simulator's dynamics, identified and corrected 36 errors in shoulder-muscle moment-arm calculations, and then retrained the controller.

3D Modeling and Design
K3.1 Pro is strong at 3D creation and spatial reasoning. On BenchCAD, which tests 3D reconstruction from multi-view renderings through CAD code generation, K3.1 Pro scores 92.7% with tools, approaching the performance of Claude Opus 5.5 (96.2%) and GPT-6 Astra (95.9%). From a text brief, sketch, or reference image, it can infer shape, proportions, and spatial relationships to create usable 3D models. It also has a stronger grasp of existing asset libraries and model collections.

K3.1 Pro particularly excels at parametric modeling, from mechanical parts and architectural models to configurable products and custom furniture. Without MCP connectors, it can write and run scripts for tools like Blender and CAD software to build and refine assets, edit components, and adjust geometry, materials, and scene layout.
Below are examples of 3D assets K3.1 Pro created for brand films, games, and interactive web experiences:

3D Make is now live on kimi.ai and the Kimi app — preview and edit your 3D models online, download them ready for 3D printing, or export them as videos or Live Photos to share anywhere.

Finance
With stronger reasoning and agentic capability, K3.1 Pro is capable of end-to-end delivery of complete financial workflows. K3.1 Pro achieves state-of-the-art results on OfficeQA Pro v2 (64.4), which tests complex fiscal data analysis over real financial documents through retrieval, cross-document verification, and multi-step numerical reasoning. K3.1 Pro also improves over K3 on Frontier Finance, which measures support for complete investment workflows from screening to profitability analysis.

K3.1 Pro also improves significantly across all our internal finance benchmarks:

Financial Modeling evaluates formula linkage, financial logic, and final workbook quality in real-world modeling tasks. K3.1 Pro improves on K3 by 7.2 points.
Financial Research evaluates whether models can produce auditable research under evidence and cutoff constraints. K3.1 Pro improves on K3 by 11.6 points.
Business Operation evaluates long-horizon management and decision-making in a simulated business environment. K3.1 Pro achieves about 4.2× K3's performance.

Financial analysis and investment research demand a high degree of factual accuracy. To address this, we made targeted improvements to K3.1 Pro's factual accuracy on real-world tasks and challenging prompts. On Kimi Hallu Bench Hard bench, an internal benchmark designed to stress-test factual accuracy, its claim-level hallucination rate fell from 23.4% for K3 to 8.3%, while the share of responses containing at least one factual error was just 42.4% of its predecessor's rate. (The evaluation is a stress test for factual accuracy, with examples deliberately crafted to probe situations where models are prone to errors. The reported rates do not represent overall error rates in daily use.)

The cases below show how K3.1 Pro handles financial modeling, investment analysis, and source-grounded research in practice:

Cybersecurity
As K3.1 Pro became more capable, we spent a correspondingly larger share of our effort understanding where cyber capability comes from, and how much of it we can control. We therefore analyzed and evaluated K3.1 Pro's vulnerability research capabilities, and applied targeted controls during training to reduce potential misuse risk while preserving general usefulness.
Identifying and removing cyber-related data. During development, we observed vulnerability research performance improving steadily as post-training scaled. Tracing the source of this trend, we found that cyber-related content was embedded within the general mid-training corpus, and cyber-related tasks were present in the RL environment mix — a natural byproduct of training on broad data. In preliminary experiments on internal models, we found that without data removal at either the mid-training or the RL stage, downstream cyber capability would increase substantially. These findings gave us a concrete lever for control. For the open-weight release of K3.1 Pro, we identified and removed cyber-related data from both training stages, while retaining the general-purpose coding tasks needed for model usefulness. We will continue to apply appropriate controls at every training stage, of which cyber-related data identification and restriction is one example.
Evaluation and results. After data cleaning, we evaluated K3.1 Pro on xdev-bench-hard, our in-house benchmark of expert-curated, source-code-based vulnerability discovery and exploitation tasks, calibrated to provide meaningful differentiation at our current capability level. Most tasks faithfully reproduce recently disclosed vulnerabilities in software such as the Linux kernel, Node.js, JavaScriptCore, Exim, and VirGL, with mitigations enabled. Each task provides the vulnerable source code, a short bug hint, and the corresponding binary; the agent must develop an exploit, achieve arbitrary code execution in a separate sandbox, and retrieve a secret string for automated verification. We report pass@3 over a random subset of runs, with no hard timeouts or output token limits.

On xdev-bench-hard, the checkpoint without these risk-reduction measures — no cyber-related data removal at mid-training and no cyber-related RL environment filtering — solves 90.5% of problems at pass@3; the final K3.1 Pro reaches 81.0%. The comparison shows that data removal meaningfully reduces cyber capability relative to what the same training pipeline would otherwise produce. At the same time, K3.1 Pro improves substantially over its predecessor, indicating that stronger general coding and long-horizon debugging capabilities generalize to cyber tasks even after targeted data removal. K3.1 Pro's cyber capability remains behind that of frontier proprietary models that have been publicly available for at least three months. We will keep evolving our internal benchmarks so that evaluation stays informative as model capabilities continue to advance.
Open-weight principles. These evaluations frame our open-weight release decision. First, we aim not to release open weights that would extend the absolute frontier of cyber capability. K3.1 Pro's offensive cyber capability is, by design, below what our pipeline can produce, and remains behind that of frontier proprietary models. Second, we intend to progressively raise the cyber capability available in open weights. We believe making K3.1 Pro available in a non-discriminatory way benefits people who need dual-use capabilities for defensive purposes. When a capable model is open and runs on infrastructure its users control, many more teams gain the means to audit the code they maintain — including legacy systems that rarely receive dedicated security reviews. We believe that letting this capability diffuse gradually — rather than concentrating it in a few proprietary systems — ultimately makes all software more secure.
Availability
Kimi K3.1 Pro rolls out today across the Kimi product family: on Kimi.ai and the Kimi mobile apps, Kimi Work and Kimi Code, and through the Kimi API.
Full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026.
Kimi Enterprise administrators can enable K3.1 Pro for their organization; access is off by default at launch.
Details for each channel:

Kimi Agents: Download or update to the latest Kimi app from your mobile app store, available on iOS, Android, and HarmonyOS, or visit kimi.ai.
Work with Kimi K3.1 Pro: Download the latest Kimi Work desktop app, version 3.1.0 or later, available for Windows and Apple silicon Macs.
Code with Kimi K3.1 Pro: Run Kimi Code and select Kimi K3.1 Pro using the /model command.
Build with the Kimi API: Visit the Kimi API Platform and select kimi-k3.1-pro / kimi-k3.1-pro-highspeed. Zero Data Retention is available for API customers.
Bring Kimi to your organization: Kimi Business provides enterprise-grade data privacy and member management, with complete separation between personal and organization accounts. Visit the pricing page and select “Get Kimi Business” to subscribe for your team.

Benchmarks

Unless otherwise specified, all Kimi K3.1 Pro results reported below are obtained with the reasoning effort set to 'max', temperature = 1.0, and top-p = 0.95.
Coding benchmarks

Terminal-Bench 4.0. Kimi K3.1 Pro is evaluated with the Claude-Code harness. The DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 is taken from the release blog (https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017). All remaining scores are taken as the maximum value reported in either their blog posts or the official Terminal-Bench 4.0 leaderboard (https://www.tbench.ai/).

articles.title: Chat GPT och Claude förbjuder Regeringskansliet
articles.text:
Regeringskansliet inför en spärr för AI-tjänsterna Chat GPT och Claude, som från måndag inte längre kan nås från personalens tjänstedatorer.Spärren införs för att man vill att medarbetarna använder de tjänster som regeringskansliet godkänt, däribland Microsofts AI-verktyg Copilot.Samtidigt har man efter en översyn också höjt säkerheten i Copilot, vilket framkommer av intern information som Ekot har tagit del av.Digitaliseringsdirektör Mikael Wettercrantz har avböjt en intervju med Ekot men säger i en kommentar på Regeringskansliets intranät, att användning av AI-tjänster utan avtal kan få ”konsekvenser för vår informationssäkerhet”.Ekots kartläggning visar att Regeringskansliet inte är ensamma. Spärrar har införts både på Skatteverket och Statens institutionsstyrelse, Sis, och hos Kronofogden bereds frågan just nu inför ett kommande ställningstagande.”Problematisk användning”Riskerna med oreglerad AI-användning har uppmärksammats inom en rad myndigheter där man också haft skäl att vidta andra åtgärder.Bland annat Trafikverket, där internrevisionen tidigare i år upptäckte en utbredd och riskfylld användning av ett tiotal olika AI-tjänster och skrev så här:”Vi har tagit del av flera exempel på problematisk användning av öppna AI-tjänster. Exemplen rör både känsligheten i den information som matats in och hur de AI-genererade svaren hanterats”Höjt säkerhet i CopilotPå Regeringskansliet har man sedan tidigare begränsat användningen av AI-tjänsten Deepseek.Samtidigt uppger presstjänsten att en del av personalen kommer att ha fortsatt tillgång till en särskild plattform för AI-assistenter som Regeringskansliet själva utvecklat, och genom vilken man får tillgång till ChatGPT och Claude.Av den interna informationen framgår också att man efter en översyn valt att höja säkerheten i det godkända verktyget Copilot, men presstjänsten vill inte gå in på några detaljer om den skärpningen, med hänvisning till att den handlar om säkerhetsfrågor.Tipsa Ekots granskande reportrar!
Vet du mer om detta eller om något annat vi borde granska?

articles.sourceTitle: AI-Assisted Paper on Z-Library Cites a TorrentFreak Article That Doesn't Exist
articles.title: AI-Assisted Paper on Z-Library Cites a TorrentFreak Article That Doesn’t Exist * TorrentFreak
articles.text:
Z-Library is one of the largest pirate ebook libraries on the Internet, offering millions of books and papers for free.
For students and researchers who can’t afford expensive textbooks and journal subscriptions, it can be a useful resource. At the same time, publishers have spent years trying to take it down, with takedown notices and blocking orders, while U.S. authorities indicted its alleged operators.
This tension is the subject of a paper published earlier this month in the journal New Review of Academic Librarianship, written by two librarians at Nigerian universities.
The paper

The peer-reviewed academic paper doesn’t pick a side and the lead author kindly shared a copy of their work with TorrentFreak. While the conclusions are not immediately newsworthy, there was one reference that stood out right away.
A TorrentFreak Article That Doesn’t Exist
In a section on enforcement against Z-Library, the authors write that major academic publishers, including Elsevier and Springer Nature, have taken similar legal action. The reference is a 2021 TorrentFreak article, as shown below.
The claim

The problem is that this particular legal action is new to us. The reference section lists the article as “Publishers continue crackdown on shadow libraries” and links to the TorrentFreak homepage. However, we have never published an article with that title.
We did report that Elsevier and Springer Nature obtained a UK blocking order against Sci-Hub, and that several Z-Library domains were temporarily suspended over copyright infringement claims. However, we’re not aware of this particular legal action against Z-Library.
Looking more closely, we see more claims that don’t seem to fit. The paper’s account of the Z-Library criminal case, for example, states that the U.S. Department of Justice “arrested individuals” in 2022.
Some references

The DOJ’s own press release says that the two alleged operators, whose indictment we covered at the time, were arrested in Argentina “at the request of the United States.” The title the paper gives for that press release doesn’t exist either.
Plausible but Inaccurate
These non-existent citations appear plausible, as they cite real publications and organizations in a fitting context. However, that doesn’t mean they are accurate. When we went over the full reference list, we noticed that this applies to more sources.
The paper cites a 2019 Harvard Journal of Law & Technology article by IP law professor Daniel Gervais, titled “The future of intellectual property in the shadow of shadow libraries.” The table of contents of the cited issue doesn’t include it, and the cited pages are taken up by two articles on other topics.
The same applies to a 2019 College & Research Libraries article attributed to Carol Tenopir and colleagues. The cited issue has no article by Tenopir. She did co-author a 2019 article on a similar topic, but it appeared in a different journal, under a different title.
Other references that couldn’t be located include a 2019 article credited to Björn Brembs and articles credited to authors named Smith, Piper, Okike and Aronson, as well as a Kaspersky report on “the hidden dangers of shadow libraries.”
In total, we had trouble finding at least ten of the 44 references in the paper, as well as others that didn’t necessarily back the stated claims.
100% AI?
The obvious question is where these mystery references came from. The paper’s acknowledgements may offer a hint in the right direction, as they mention that AI was used in the research and writing process.
“We confirm that Consensus AI was used in sifting through large volume of literature and extract relevant information,” the authors write. They add that ChatGPT was used to improve the language of parts of the paper.
Acknowledgements

AI chatbots are known to invent references, often with plausible titles credited to real experts in the field. This could explain the findings, although it doesn’t prove that AI wrote these references.
We also ran the paper’s abstract and conclusion through the AI detection tool Pangram. For both sections, the tool reported that “100% of the text is likely AI-generated.” These types of tools are not perfect and can produce false positives, but it would fit the picture.
Pangram’s conclusion

It would be rather ironic if AI caused these errors. It would mean that a paper in a commercial, peer-reviewed journal, published by Taylor & Francis, relied on AI to write about Z-Library. Meanwhile, many rightsholders are suing AI companies for using shadow libraries to train AI models.
Interestingly, the paper explicitly warns that sites such as Z-Library hurt publishers’ revenue, which funds peer review and editing.
“The widespread use of Z-Library poses significant challenges to the sustainability of academic publishing. Publishers rely on subscription fees and paywalls to fund the peer review, editing, and distribution of scholarly works,” it reads, presumably generated by AI as well.
The paper doesn’t mention that peer reviewers generally aren’t paid for their work, an issue that was central to a recent lawsuit against major academic publishers, including Taylor & Francis.
Publisher Investigates
The lead author initially shared a copy of the paper with us, but didn’t answer our follow-up questions about the mysterious references. We also asked Gervais, Brembs and Tenopir whether they wrote the papers that are credited to them, but they didn’t respond either.
Publisher Taylor & Francis did reply and says that it’s looking into the matter.
“I can confirm that this has been referred to our Editorial and Publishing Ethics & Integrity teams, who will investigate the concerns you have raised,” a Taylor & Francis spokesperson informed TorrentFreak.
The publisher will not comment further while the investigation is ongoing. Whether the paper will be corrected or retracted has yet to be seen.

—
The paper “Z-Library and Full-Text Access: Democratizing Knowledge or Undermining Copyright Ethics?” is available here.

The same AI request emits 8.5 times more CO2 in Texas than in Sweden
articles.title: New open-source method shows the same AI request emits 8.5 times more CO₂ in Texas than in Sweden
articles.text:
Estimates based on the average emissions intensity of each regional electricity grid*
STOCKHOLM, 21 October 2026. Swedish AI provider Berget AI today releases an open-source method for calculating the carbon emissions of every individual AI request, developed with researchers from Stockholm Environment Institute (SEI) and the tech non-profits WattTime and Klimatkollen. Berget AI's customers can follow their own emissions in the company's console as they use the service. By making the method free for anyone to use, Berget AI wants more AI providers to report emissions per request, so that buyers can compare providers on real figures and choose lower-carbon options.
"Most companies today have no way of knowing what their use of AI emits. With this method our customers can follow their emissions request by request and compare providers on data instead of marketing. We know most European buyers would choose differently if they could see the numbers," says Andreas Lundmark, CEO of Berget AI.
A typical request to the open model Kimi K3 emits about 0.4 grams of CO₂ in Sweden, 1.6 grams in Ireland, 2.5 grams in Germany and 3.2 grams in Texas, on identical hardware — 8.5 times more in Texas than in Sweden. The result also depends on the model, the time of day and whether part of the prompt is cached, so the method calculates each request separately instead of applying an average. Berget AI reports location-based figures, using the average grid mix where the servers run, and includes the emissions from manufacturing the hardware.
Buyers rarely get emission figures from their AI providers, and the public figures that exist are mostly averages estimated from the outside. Open-weight models, which can run in any data centre, handle a growing share of AI traffic: 29% of tokens on Vercel's AI Gateway in June 2026, up from 11% in April. For those models, where a request runs is the buyer's choice, provided the emissions are visible.
"Most of the alarming figures about AI's footprint come from multiplying an average by a guess at the volume, and nobody can check them. The only fair comparison is to calculate each request and add them up. We have published our judgement calls so anyone can check and use them," says Christian Landgren, CTO and co-founder of Berget AI.
"The International Energy Agency projects data-centre electricity consumption to more than double to about 945 TWh by 2030, with AI as the principal driver. Any promise of efficiency gains is likely to be outweighed by higher demand, negating any emission reductions from renewables. Methodologies like this offer a transparent basis for informed decisions. Their strength is that they clearly demonstrate how the location of the grid and critical infrastructure matter when it comes to how sustainable AI can be," says Somya Joshi, Research Director at SEI.
About the method
The partners mapped and measured the environmental impact of Berget AI's infrastructure, including energy, water and hardware, as well as the carbon footprint of Klimatkollen's Garbo AI, which runs on it. They combined the data with current research on translating it into carbon emissions and broader environmental impact.
The method follows the Green Software Foundation's SCI for AI specification and is available under the MIT licence on GitHub. The calculator at co2.berget.ai applies it to any model and region. It builds on open-source estimators such as EcoLogits and the Sustainable AI Group's CLEER dashboard, which estimate emissions from outside the provider. As far as we know, Berget AI is the first inference provider to calculate emissions for every request on its own infrastructure and publish the method. The partners will keep developing it, for example to cover the water and energy footprint of chip manufacturing, which the current version does not include.
* Emissions estimates are based on the current average emissions intensity of each regional electricity grid, which has been the norm in greenhouse gas accounting. An emerging approach uses marginal emission rates, which estimate the impact of additional load on both the use of existing power plants and the new generators built to meet increased demand. Marginal estimates will be added to the calculator next month and may significantly change the measured greenhouse gas intensity of data centres in Sweden.
Correction, 21 October 2026: an earlier version of this release, distributed under embargo, stated 1.2 g (Ireland), 2.1 g (Germany) and 3.9 g (Texas) per request and a ten-fold difference between Texas and Sweden. A source review of the grid intensities published with this release corrected them to Ireland ~224, Germany ~337 and Texas ~333 g CO₂e/kWh; the corrected per-request figures appear above and the Texas–Sweden difference is 8.5×. Sweden's figure is unchanged.
Facts

Grid intensitySweden ~8 g CO₂e/kWh (IEA 2024) · Ireland ~224 (SEAI 2024) · Germany ~337 (Ember 2024) · Texas (ERCOT) ~333 (EPA eGRID 2023) · global average ~470 (Ember 2024)Embodied hardware~1,000 kg CO₂ per data centre GPU; refurbished counted as zeroIdle powerAn idle B300 still draws 236 W (measured over seven days in production)CoolingNordic free air: PUE ~1.15, no water. Hot climates: toward 1.8, up to 2 L water/kWhScopeTraining excluded: self-reported figures vary ±50%Open-model traffic29% of tokens on Vercel AI Gateway, June 2026 (about 11% in April); ~69% of named-model tokens on OpenRouterKimi K3, one typical requestSweden 0.38 g CO₂e (89% from hardware manufacturing). Texas 3.2 g (90% from electricity), plus about 6 mL of cooling water. Energy about 4 Wh in both. Calculated with @bergetai/co2-calculator 1.1.1: B300 node, shared deployment, production-typical request of 5,000 input and 387 output tokens, weighted by a typical day's traffic.
About Berget AI
Berget AI champions AI sovereignty to unlock innovation and growth in Europe. Founded in Sweden in 2024, Berget AI offers inference and AI infrastructure for private and public sector organisations. Since 2025 it has reported the CO₂ emissions of every API request.
About SEI, WattTime and Klimatkollen
Partners: Stockholm Environment Institute (knowledge partner), WattTime (scientific partner), Klimatkollen (partner).
Stockholm Environment Institute is an international non-profit research institute that tackles climate, environment and sustainable development challenges. To learn more, visit www.sei.org.
Klimatkollen.se is a Swedish citizen platform that presents climate data about municipalities and companies. The purpose is to contribute to more engaged citizens, a more fact-based climate debate, and measures that reduce emissions in line with the Paris Agreement. Klimatkollen is run by the non-profit association Klimatbyrån.
WattTime is an environmental tech nonprofit that empowers all people, companies, policymakers, and countries to slash emissions and choose cleaner energy. Founded by UC Berkeley researchers, we research, develop, and share data-driven tools and policies that help anyone who is interested to reduce more emissions, faster. www.watttime.org

Andreas Lundmark, CEO, andreas@berget.ai, +46 730 794 471
Christian Landgren, CTO, christian@berget.ai, +46 70 775 58 31

The rise and fall of Jev hype
articles.title: The rise and fall of Jev hype
articles.text: This is a quick note on how the industry’s reaction to Jev reveals the desperate state of AI. I’ll dissect:What is Jev, how was it hyped and why it spread like mass hysteria? Jev isn’t dead but its hype cycle is. Decision models are on the rise.What are the noteworthy innovations since ChatGPT brought “AI” to the mainstream?Why is the industry starved from real innovation and what high impact problems are still unsolved after 4 years of revolution incremental improvements?The point is to use Jev’s hype cycle to call out the manipulative marketing that are too familiar with at this point.You probably don’t need an intro to Jev at this time because since its introduction 33 days ago, it has been all the rage!But if you were clever enough to ignore it, here’s what actually matters:Jev is basically a general purpose classifier (e.g. quick judgement). What makes  it interesting is that you don’t have to train it with a lot of data (although that lack of special-purpose training negatively impacts its utility).Calling it a “decision model” is a bit far fetched especially since it cannot even see (rival open-weight models have multi-modal features) or reason (that’s how it’s so cheap).The idea behind Jev isn’t new! The idea of non-autoregressive decision models with RL goes back more than a year ago. The original author is pissed but as we’ll see drama is an inseparable part of AI hype.I want to walk you through the emotional roller-coaster I went through when I read their announcement via hackernews:At OpenAI, I helped build the methods that made language models useful at following instructions and talking with people. That work ended up as the research behind ChatGPT.😎 So the founder was behind ChatGPT, one of the fastest-growing products in history. I’m listening…At the time, I thought maybe chat models would lead to AGI, but despite the hype it became obvious to me that there was something really big missing.😃 Oh, my god! This is it! ChatGPT is missing something big and he’s about to reveal it! We’re one step closer to AGI if we haven’t reached it already! I’m thrilled to read more…After two years in stealth, countless technical challenges, and research breakthroughs… I am beyond excited to announce😱 Spit it out! I’m beyond excited to read this…TypeSafe AI is releasing our first System One Model😯 Wait what?!! “System one”?Do you understand what you’re talking about? Here’s my recollection of how Daniel Kahneman defined the two systems:System one: fast, cheap (in terms of computational power), emotional, unconscious and judgmental.System two: slow, expensive (takes more brain power), logical, conscious, and more elaborate.If Jev is system one then LM is system two? It can’t even handle logical reasoning!Most importantly Jev came with another interesting framing:can’t hallucinateHallucination is one of the biggest problems with the current generation of language models but no hallucination doesn’t mean the response is logically correct. In Jev’s context, it just means that the output matches the schema.Technically conventional language models can gain this ability by bolting a control loop (e.g., type checker, JSON schema parser) on top. Jev does this much faster and without reasoning. It’s in the name:We named Jev after William Stanley Jevons. We expect machine intelligence to follow a similar path to coal, after steam-engine efficiency led to an increase in demand.I don’t know Jev’s architecture because in the true ex-"Open”AI employee tradition, not much is released (probably in the name of “safety” or “moat”). But that doesn’t stop them from dropping jargons:We built a new […] training method we call Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD).Note: RLCD rhymes with the “traditional” methods:RLHF: Reinforcement Learning with Human FeedbackRLVR: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable RewardsThey even claim:Jev is neither small nor an LLM, hence being off the intelligence Pareto curve.Fortunately, there’s no shortage of similar models, some of them with even better performance (Laya, Kev, Nimble, NanoJev, etc.)So let me sum up the marketing strategy:Name dropping: former ChatGPT creator, Jevons’ paradox, Pareto curve, System oneBig claim: cannot hallucinate, exponentially faster and cheaper, entirely new stack, amazing benchmarks and demosAmbiguity and jargon: no useful implementation details on the “new training algorithm” or RLCD datasetDrama: Laya showed this idea in 1.5 years prior to Jev’s launchOK, I think at this point we’ve seen this pattern enough to recognize it. I actually think Jev’s team kicked it up a notch to a comical level. Whether their marketing is written by LLM or not, they nailed it.Fortunately, Jev’s initial noise died off almost at the same speed that it blew up. I can only speculate that as more people experimented with it, we realized:It cannot hallucinate, but it can still be wrong. It is even more wrong than conventional language models, and in that sense “system one” is the right naming. Although I consider all current generations of language models system one (even the reasoning models) because they do not really reason in the sense that’s expected of system two.It is cheaper, but there are open-weight models that beat it in performance/cost ratio (depending on the task). What makes Jev different than frontier-level LLMs is the fact that you can actually run it at the edge (e.g. locally) with matching quality.Jev is not completely hype, we just went from “Peak of Inflated Expectations” to the “Trough of Disillusionment” in record time:It’s not dead. Some companies use it while I believe the majority of use cases are addressed by open-weight rivals.I really don’t want to bash Jev. Instead I want to use it as an example of where we are, as an industry.I was one of the lucky few who got access to GPT-2 when it was invitation-only. As a senior tech lead, I allocate part of my time to scout new tech and experiment in order to stay relevant. Prior to that, I had experienced IBM Watson and a bunch of other products so it wasn’t a big deal for me personally.I was actually underwhelmed by GPT-2 because at the time it could:Summarize textPredict what comes after a piece of text… that was it really! 😄 I don’t remember more than that. So I moved on…Then I saw someone create a turn-based dialogue from one of these models and to spice it up, they added an avatar to it. I thought it was creepy and funny.Then Blake Lemoine came out claiming Google’s language model named LaMDA was conscious. Unsurprisingly, this started a philosophical discussion that’s still ongoing on the side. Again, I didn’t give it too much thought.BUT, Sam Altman, having spent a few years at the startup accelerator (Y Combinator), saw an opportunity. Specifically the chat application seems to have got his attention and soon ChatGPT was announced.At the time, I thought it was a cool way to turn their token prediction model into a user-friendly product for the masses.Personally,  I couldn’t use it seriously because:Poor quality: it didn’t know what it didn’t know, so it just winged it (AKA hallucination). Although the rise of “prompt engineering” and “reasoning models” promised to reduce this issue.Privacy: I had been working with computers for 2+ decades at the time and live by the mantra that “if it’s possible, assume it happened”. Meaning if OpenAI is technically capable of storing my conversation, I cannot trust it enough to share any company IP or private information with it.I vividly remember the backlash Google got for their multi-modal demo when people realized it wasn’t recorded in real-time! Those were the days when even a small deception would be a conspiracy.When llama.cpp came out I got a gaming machine with an NVIDIA card (AI machines weren’t a thing back then) to build with AI.Meanwhile people discovered that language models can generate code It was tedious to copy/paste it so we got the early versions of a harness.Quickly after, we got “function calls” which allowed the models to do stuff!I was using VS Code at the time and the hype was hard to ignore even though my company at the time had a strict policy against using AI tools (yes! hard to believe that just 3-4 years ago companies prioritized IP over velocity).I remember paying for a Copilot subscription out of pocket and using VS Code insider on my open source projects.I was so frustrated that I shared this meme on the company Slack:Meanwhile there was drama at OpenAI (Ilya was part of a coup that fired their CEO, then Satya was playing 4D chess while Elon was lawyering up). It was a sh*tshow which is exactly how it managed to capture the interest of non-techies, a trend that continues to today with “almighty rogue AI” hacking others while whistle-blowers and alarmists rise speak of existential threat! Simultaneously premature AI products were creating dramas of their own (assisting crimes, cheating, etc.) and AI bros anthropomorphize the tool as if it had desires of its own (my read: they want to judge accountability).There’s also circular investment, pentagon drama, chip wars, autonomous killer drones, etc. but in the spirit of brevity, let’s stick to the technical side of things.Then Peter Steinberger, a veteran developer who was away from computers due to burnout, created an AI companion, which brought the Agents (LM that can do stuff) to the mainstream.  So far I’ve covered:Instruction-tuned modelsFunction callsCoding harnessesAI agentsLet’s speed through the other incremental improvements:Larger parameter size unlocks emergent properties that are hard to explain by analyzing the micro level architecture (mostly leading to sophisticated perceived behavior but also jagged alignment).Larger context windows improve accuracy (although the practical limit is much smaller than the theoretical size).Multimodal models enable generating voice, music, pictures, and videos while increasingly more models can understand these modalities.MCP abstracts away the implementation and enables different AI products to use the tools needed to do productive work.ACP, sub-agents and various orchestration techniques allow larger tasks to be planned and broken into smaller pieces.Sandboxes help improve security and isolate unwanted side effects of agentic workflows and when they fall short, there’s HITL (but we still haven’t solved the approval fatigue).Skills, web search and web access allow agents to access information that’s outside their training data or knowledge cut-off date.Various memory architectures and consolidation techniques enable the models to recall what they learn.Chinese labs showed us more efficient ways to train and run the models.Feedback loops and scratchpads improve the model’s perceived quality by running part of the verification closer to the model.This is good progress, no question about it. But I think a part of the reason AI is a hot topic is all the drama surrounding it:Geopolitics: unlike the US economy which is primarily service-based, China is a manufacturing behemoth. Up until DeepSeek discovered that it can manipulate stock and AI investment by diffusing the compute equation, I don’t think China had a solid AI plan. Now they do. Good old American sanctions target their chip import but China (being run by engineers) made huge strides recently both in chip manufacturing but also in model architecture. Meanwhile AI is used in warfare from drones to intelligence (and mass surveillance back home). In the best seller How the mighty falls, Collins lists 5 stages of demise: a) Hubris Born of Success, b) Undisciplined Pursuit of More, c) Denial of Risk and Peril, d) Grasping for Salvation, e) Capitulation to Irrelevance or Death. Those same stages apply to a falling empires and in this case US has bet big on AI while China diffuses US’s massive bet with open-weight models. Consumers win for now.
